blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Project Q9 costs 200, 500 and 300 in its first, second and third year of work, and may start in 2028 or 2029. In the 2030 spend expression, what are the coefficients of x[Q9,2028] and x[Q9,2029]?

options.text: 300 and 500, since 2030 is the third and the second year of work for those starts
options.says: Right: a 2028 start is in its third year in 2030, a 2029 start in its second.

options.text: 500 and 300, since 2030 is the second and the third year of work for those starts
options.says: This reverses the offsets: the earlier start is further into its profile.

options.text: 1,000 and 0, since the whole cost is charged in the year the project starts
options.says: That is the lump shortcut; the cost lands in the years of work.

options.text: 1,000 and 1,000, since a project's cost counts in every year it is active
options.says: Each year carries only that year's slice of the profile, not the whole cost.

origin.section: A Project's Cost Lands in the Years It Is Worked On

questions.stem: A model writes the yearly budget rows with one triple loop and a regional cap with a second, copied loop. Months later someone fixes an off-by-one in the first loop only. What happens?

options.text: The two rules still agree about each project's spend, since their data is shared
options.says: They read the same data through different code, and only one copy of the code was fixed.

options.text: The solver reports the model infeasible, since its rows now differ
options.says: Different rows are still valid rows; the model solves and quietly uses two notions of spend.

options.text: The two rules now disagree about each project's spend, since their code differs
options.says: Right: two definitions of spend drift apart; one shared expression per year avoids it.

options.text: The solver merges the two rules, since presolve removes repeated rows
options.says: The rows are not repeats once they differ, and presolve cannot know which one is right.

origin.section: Build Spend as an Expression Once, and Every Budget Rule Reuses It

questions.stem: A five-year plan built with every project's cost charged to its start year shows every year within budget. Finance spreads the real costs and finds the last two years over budget. Why the last years?

options.text: Projects started earlier are discounted there, and the model valued those years too high
options.says: Discounting changes NPV, not spend; the overrun is spending the model did not count.

options.text: Projects started earlier still spend there, and the model filled those years with new starts
options.says: Right: the lump model believed those later costs were already paid, so it added more work on top.

options.text: Later budgets are always smaller, so any plan overspends at the end
options.says: The overrun comes from uncounted spend, not from the budgets' size.

options.text: Later budgets are spread too, so the model counted them twice
options.says: Budgets are data per year; only the projects' costs were mis-spread.

origin.section: Charging Everything to the Start Year Breaks the Budget the Plan Claims to Respect
